newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right stages racially-charged protest.
newsitem.headline: French far-right stages racially-charged protest.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, ignoring charges of racism, led about 6,500 supporters on a tightly-policed march on Saturday to mourn a white teenager allegedly killed by a youth of Arab origin.

Backed by supporters in the Mediterranean port of Marseille shouting "France for the French" and "Le Pen for president", Le Pen blasted the state over the fatal stabbing of 14-year-old Nicolas Bourgat on Monday.

"The main responsibility lies with the decadent, impotent state, which was incapable of guaranteeing basic freedoms for its citizens, first among them security," he told a rally that broke up with scuffles with counter-protesters.

Earlier, Le Pen led his supporters, estimated by police at about 6,500, in bright sunshine from the old port to the office of the government Prefect under tight police guard as others booed and denounced them as racists.

Banners included "Protect our children" and "Immigration equals insecurity". Nicolas's father, a local doctor, was among many who pleaded against Le Pen's march, saying he did not want his son's death hijacked for political ends.
As the rally broke up, a few of Le Pen's supporters traded punches with opponents before police stepped in. They also yelled "Go home!" and other insults at a group of Africans.
Le Pen, already at the centre of a furore this week after he openly espoused a doctrine of racial inequality, reiterated that "every day the facts show us that races are different".
A 15-year-old French boy of North African origin, named only as Ktab, was placed under investigation on suspicion of murdering Nicolas on Friday. He is being held in detention.

Church bells rang out across Marseille at 2.30 p.m. (1230 GMT), calling for five minutes' silence to coincide with the start of Nicolas's funeral in a Marseille church. Several thousand people crowded the streets around the church.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said he hoped that a draft bill tightening laws against racism would be ready to be passed to parliament next month.

The planned laws would make indirect provocations to racial discrimination, hatred or violence into crimes, he told the daily Liberation. And Toubon said the government also wanted to stiffen sentences for racist crimes.

Le Pen, aged 68, has been under fire for saying that racial inequality was a "fact" and that some civilisations, like the French, are superior. One Socialist opposition politician called this week for the National Front to be outlawed.
Toubon condemned Le Pen's remarks as "totally reprehensible" but said he could not be prosecuted under existing laws, saying they can only sanction direct provocations to racial hatred.
On Friday, French President Jacques Chirac visited the former Nazi extermination camp at Auschwitz during a visit to Poland and called for vigilance against possible future anti-Semitism.
Le Pen won 15 percent in last year's presidential election by blaming immigration for unemployment, crime and insecurity and calling for three million immigrants to be sent home.
The National Front is vying with Juppe's Gaullist RPR party and the opposition Communists for the working-class vote in the run-up to parliamentary elections in 1998.
